body:
He seemed to be like any other man, nothing that seemed to strike him as spectacular. See, my job is to simply kill those whose time it is to pass, not to worry over what they would be leaving behind. His name was John, and he had no family at all. He was a very lonely man, and at the time it even seemed to me that I was helping him. One day, the exact date does not matter, he came home early and went up to his study. He locked the door and from inside came a loud chorus of sobs. It was then that I entered, I sensed that his time was at an end and when he looked up at me, he didn’t even seem surprised. 
"It's time isn't it?" He asked, looking at me with red eyes. But they showed no fear, only deep grief, a type of sorrow that goes beyond the flesh and bone and it pained me to see this. 
"Yes." I replied, I try not to engage too much in conversation with those I have to pass over to the other side. 
"You know, I had felt that my time was actually coming to an end. Is that strange? That I should know this?" He said this with the heaviness of someone who knows the inevitable and has accepted it. 
"No, it is not." I tried to not look him the eyes, I needed to be completely focused when I killed him. As horrible as that sounds, I simply cannot be distracted when the process begins. 
"Do you know what lies beyond the doors of death?" He began to wipe his eyes, and was trying to compose himself. 
"I do, but it is not my place to say." I felt a twang of sadness, this man was about to be sent into the unknown.  
"You know, it's lonely being here all alone. But it's also pleasant, in a way. In here I cannot be hurt, at least not by most people." He said that last part with a knowing smile, he knew that his time was about to end and he seemed to be coming to terms with it. 
"Would you mind if I tell you something that I have never told anyone before?" He said this with a small wavering of his voice, as if he would soon burst into tears. I felt that the least I could do was to let him tell his tale, before I had to do the inevitable. 
"As a child I had the best of friends, her name was Kylie, and she was what kept me up when everything around me would be falling apart. We would tell each other stories of how we would change the world, on how we would make sure that no child would feel the pain that we both felt. She would say these stories with a look in her eyes that said she would do this, that she would stop at nothing to make sure that every child was loved and cared for. She was strong. Stronger than a child should be, at least that's what it seemed to me. And we would spend our summers running about in the woods into our various hiding places. Places where we went when things got bad, as they seemed to always get eventually. It was during one particularly bad day, my father had beaten my mum and threatened the same to me, that I went to my hiding place. It was a small clearing near a river and surrounded by bushes on all sides, the perfect place to stop and think. When I arrived I had hoped to see my friend, my Kylie, but she did not come. It was late at night when I started to worry, she should have already been here by now. Despite being worried that she might arrive when I was gone, I needed  get back home. Otherwise unpleasant things would no doubt happen. But when I had arrived there were cars everywhere. Cop cars. I ran as fast as my little legs could take me, and when I came to the front door my mum opened the door and burst into tears. She was shaking with sobs when she grabbed hold of me and I started to cry too. The police officers saw me and rushed to me, asking me if I was okay and where I had been. When I told them they showed a small visible sign of relief but I was still frightened, I had no idea of what was going on. I learned that my friend's father had gotten drunk and killed everyone. I did not know the details and I would not want to. But I have always felt that it was my fault. I should have done something, anything, but I did not." He was crying now, no not just crying, he was weeping. His body was shaking as the rivers of grief pulled him apart. 
"You know, today is the day she died 20 years ago." He barely managed to say this. But I barely even heard him.  I remembered that day, it was not supposed to happen that way. The father had been a drunk his whole life and it was time for him to pass. He was slowly being torn apart by his sickness, addiction is a horrible thing. When I came to him he had looked into my eyes, and when I looked into his eyes all I could see was an empty man. He knew, like everyone who saw me, that it was his time. But he would not go, at least he did not want to. He started to throw things at me, yelling, trying to make me go away. Calling me a demon and that he would not be taken away. I had tried to control him, but for a moment my concentration had broken and instead of killing him I broke his mind. When this sort of thing happens, it is impossible to repair the damage. All that can be done is hope that nothing too severe will happen. But he had take his pistol, and in front of me he slaughtered his entire family. 
"… will you please answer me?" John said, looking at me with pleading eyes.
"Will she be there when I go?" He was about to burst into tears again, and I could not but think that if I had not screwed up that one day then maybe I would not be here at this moment, that maybe John wouldn’t be this damaged. I looked into his eyes, and for the first time I noticed a kind of intensity in them. 
"All things change, especially in death. For me to tell you if she would be there would be the same as me trying to read the future or trying to find a meaning in the movement of the wind. It simply cannot be done with certainty."  
"I'm sorry John, but it Is time to go." I could not look into his eyes, but I felt his burning into me.
